entry.title: Watching AI Agents Work Together in Games
entry.content:
YC Labs’ experiments with AI agents in games reminded me of the multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) I used to study. I liked that I could follow what the agents did, mistakes included.

Minecraft: a civilisation in three hours

In one run, 50 agents had three hours to build a civilisation. They formed a hierarchy, rationed food, and sent about 5,900 messages. After a hard first night, they grew cautious and sheltered more. Their shared files held food queues and rules about who could take supplies.

One detail stayed with me: an agent picking up food did not mean the recipient had it. The agents had to check who had eaten before calling a delivery complete.

This is a software handoff problem. A message saying a task is done can drift from the actual state, and the next agent may act on the message without checking. When several agents rely on the same wrong report, a small error spreads.

Competitive games: Bed Wars and Mindustry

YC also recorded competitive Minecraft games, such as Bed Wars.

In Mindustry, teams competed. YC reported that the GPT agents split ownership into smaller pieces, while the Claude agents relied more on a leader. The GPT team won the seven-game series 6–1. That score describes this setup, not how the models compare on other tasks. See the interactive Mindustry replay.

The replays make the coordination easy to follow. A team must divide responsibilities, share resources, and react when a plan fails. Those choices shape what each agent can do, even with one shared objective.

Why MARL felt harder

What made MARL hard for me was that an agent’s best action depends on what the others do, while they are also learning and changing.

Game theory describes incentives, strategies, and equilibria. MARL adds how agents learn to act from experience, often with incomplete information, so there is a learning process to account for as well as a solution. That was the part I found more involved. Game theory itself can be extremely difficult; I am comparing with fixed optimisation, not ranking the two subjects.

In simple optimisation, the objective and constraints are fixed and you search for a good solution. In a multi-agent setting, an action’s outcome depends on other agents’ actions, and in MARL those agents may adapt at the same time. A strategy that beat yesterday’s behaviour may fail against today’s.

An equilibrium describes a relationship between strategies. It does not explain how agents with limited observations and finite experience reach it; exploration, learning rules, and information all shape that path.

Changing policies

One issue is non-stationarity. To one learner, the other learners are part of the environment. As their policies change, earlier experience loses value. Lowe and colleagues discuss this in Multi-Agent Actor-Critic for Mixed Cooperative-Competitive Environments.

The textbook example below (not YC data) shows two agents learning Rock–Paper–Scissors with WoLF-PHC, each adapting to the other.

Credit and partial information

Then there is credit. A shared reward tells the team it succeeded, not which actions helped. A team can win because one agent acted well much earlier, another kept a supply chain going, or an opponent blundered; the final score does not separate these. This is the credit-assignment problem tackled by methods such as counterfactual multi-agent policy gradients. Delayed rewards also force the algorithm to link outcomes to actions further back in time.

Partial observation adds more. An agent may see only locally and must act without knowing what teammates know, so two agents with aligned goals can decide differently. Messages help, but can be late, incomplete, or outdated. The free textbook Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Foundations and Modern Approaches covers these questions alongside the game-theoretic foundations.

Coordination without online learning

I see related coordination questions in YC’s experiments, but the runs are not evidence of online reinforcement learning. The report describes coding agents using tools, messages, scripts, and memory. Revising a plan or script mid-match does not update a model’s weights.

This matters when reading adaptation. A coding agent can read an error, change a script, and retry while the model stays fixed. In MARL training, the learner updates the policy itself from experience. Both change the next interaction, by different mechanisms.

The overlap is the coordination problem. Who has the information a decision needs? How does one agent’s action change another’s options? Does a local success help the team? These apply whether agents talk in natural language, use learned policies, or both.

Coordination also costs something. More agents mean more interactions and more demand on shared resources. A team may get more done, or spend its effort on conflicts and updates. Message volume alone cannot tell you which; compare the result with the resources used.

The original report has replays, messages, and links to the code. The food-delivery records show a failed handoff up close; the Mindustry matches show coordination under competition. Together, they made MARL easier to picture than a win rate alone.

The diagrams are reproduced without redrawing from the authors’ original lecture materials for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Foundations and Modern Approaches, with the MIT licence and copyright notice.

entry.title: Why I’m Still Learning Maths
entry.content:
I studied Applied Maths and Computing, so whether maths is still worth learning is a personal question for me.

OpenAI’s announcements about Navier–Stokes and the Exponential Time Hypothesis make it easy to wonder where humans fit. If you are about to spend years studying mathematics, what are you working towards when machines produce results like these?

The Navier–Stokes equations describe fluid motion. OpenAI claimed a proof that, under a smooth external force, initially smooth three-dimensional motion can develop a singularity in finite time. Researchers have since questioned whether the Lean formalization matches the written proof. That does not make the result false, but the computer-checked version cannot yet be treated as verification of the written argument.

The ETH announcement is a different kind of problem. The hypothesis says, roughly, that deciding whether a 3-SAT Boolean formula can be satisfied takes exponential time in the worst case. OpenAI’s published notes describe a subexponential algorithm. Its bound is still superpolynomial, so it does not settle P versus NP or give us a fast everyday tool.

I want to understand those details. Reading that a problem is solved tells me little about the assumptions, the method, or what someone could build from it. Even judging how much weight an announcement deserves takes some knowledge of the maths.

Grant Sanderson’s video on AI and mathematics compares practising maths to going to the gym. A machine can do the work faster, but doing it yourself still builds your own ability.

Watch the full video on YouTube.

That matches how I build software with AI. I want to understand the assumptions behind an answer, follow the reasoning, and check whether it applies to my problem. An answer I cannot explain leaves me dependent on whoever, or whatever, produced it.

It is tempting to stop once the code runs. If an AI suggests an algorithm, I want to know why it works and which inputs might cause trouble. If it proposes a mathematical model, I want to know what it assumes about the thing it represents. A convincing explanation can still leave out a condition that matters.

That takes practice. Following a solution is easier than reconstructing it later. Working the problem myself shows me where I am confused: sometimes a definition I have used too loosely, sometimes algebra I followed without seeing why anyone chose that approach.

That is part of what makes maths useful beyond a particular course or theorem. It trains me to be precise about a question, keep track of assumptions, and find where an argument stops working. I want those habits when I use AI too.

I also like how maths finds uses far from the questions people started with. Elliptic curves appear in Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem and in cryptographic systems such as ECDSA. Elliptic-curve cryptography predates Wiles’s proof, so one did not come from the other. Both build on an older body of mathematics.

To follow the connection, I need to know what an elliptic curve is, how its points can be added, and how changing the number system changes the arithmetic. The picture below shows the real-number case. Cryptography takes that arithmetic into finite fields, where the points are discrete.

ECDSA uses elliptic-curve arithmetic to create and verify digital signatures. I could use a library without knowing any of that. Learning the maths lets me understand the design, read its assumptions, and ask better questions about it, even if I never prove a new theorem about elliptic curves.

Try the curve in Desmos, explore finite-field arithmetic, or read the cryptography reference.

Complex numbers have a similar story. They emerged through work on algebraic equations and later became part of the language of quantum mechanics. Geometry beyond Euclid became part of how general relativity describes gravity. The people working on the original questions could not have laid out those later uses.

So I am reluctant to judge maths only by its immediate applications. The methods developed along the way, or a link to another subject, may prove useful. When AI produces a new result, I want to understand what else we might do with the ideas behind it. Explaining those ideas, testing their limits, and finding where they apply could be years of worthwhile work.

I would not claim that asking questions or building theories will always be uniquely human, and Grant considers that too. His argument leaves room for much more capable machines while still valuing the experience of learning maths.

He also argues this is a good time to enter the field. The community knows it needs to change, so newcomers have a chance to influence how mathematics is explained and how contributions are recognised. I like that his answer has room for people who enjoy teaching, visualising, applying, or understanding mathematics, not only proving theorems.

I do not take that as a promise that a maths career will be easy or that academic life will survive unchanged. I can see a reason to learn without knowing what jobs or research will look like in ten years. I want to understand more of the systems I work with, and maths keeps giving me things to understand.

That makes this a good time to keep learning. I can ask AI about a step I do not follow, request a smaller example, or explore a connection. I can ask for the same idea algebraically and geometrically, then compare both with a textbook or another source.

I also need to leave myself enough work to learn from. A complete solution given too early makes it hard to tell whether I could have found the next step myself. I would rather try the problem, ask for a hint when I get stuck, and spend time with the part that confused me.

So: try a problem before reading the solution. Use AI when I get stuck. Then close the answer and see whether I can explain the reasoning without it.

entry.title: A Design Checklist You Can Give Your AI
entry.content:
I wanted a link I could paste into an AI conversation to have it check an interface, explain what needs work, and suggest fixes.

Design Guide for AI is that link. It has 138 checklists and 908 items from Checklist Design, plus instructions for choosing checks and reporting what the agent can verify.

Give the agent a starting point

Open the guide page, copy the review prompt, and add your website, screenshots, or project files. The assistant needs the interface as well as the guide.

A shorter prompt:

Read https://jienweng.github.io/design/llms.txt and follow its review protocol. Review this interface using the relevant checklists. Account for every selected item, cite evidence, and separate observed problems from checks you cannot verify. Suggest fixes before changing anything.

Then add the interface, narrowed where you can: “Review this sign-up form” works better than “Check my app.”

The LLM entry point has the review instructions and links to each checklist, so an agent fetches only what it needs. The complete text guide holds everything, for offline use or assistants that cannot follow links. If it cannot open links at all, paste in the relevant text.

What the agent should return

First, the agent should say which checklists it selected and why. A form might need the input-field, button, submission, and validation checklists; an empty-state screenshot needs a different set.

Each item gets a status: Present, Partial, Missing, Not applicable, or Unverified. The report gives evidence and location, proposes fixes, reconciles item counts, and lists anything skipped.

A screenshot can show that an email field has no visible label. It cannot show how a screen reader announces the field. The report should separate the two and name the test still needed.

Optional elements are similar. A checklist might mention an illustration, but a small utility form may not need one. The agent should say so rather than add decoration to satisfy a list.

Where the checklists come from

Checklist Design publishes an official agent-skill repository under the MIT license. I used that bundle rather than scrape the website.

The items, descriptions, and tips are their work. I added the website presentation, shareable text files, review protocol, and checks for incomplete reports. The license and source manifest credit the original authors and pin the source commit.

It covers design systems, web apps, mobile apps, websites, and user flows. It is a snapshot; source changes need review before import.

What I tested

I ran three fresh agent reviews, each with different evidence: a form’s source code, an empty-state screenshot, and a modal’s source with recorded browser observations. The reviewers did not see the expected answers.

They reported all 37 selected items and matched the expected outcomes in 19 checks. They found the four planted problems: a missing field label, missing supporting text, no modal close action, and a modal that overflowed on mobile. They left unseen behavior unverified and respected the request to omit decorative illustrations.

These were three controlled cases with one model, not proof of how every model handles a large product or an ambiguous screenshot. The report validator checks item IDs, missing rows, totals, and completion claims. A person still judges whether the evidence supports the findings and the fixes help.

To try it, copy the prompt from the guide and start with one screen or flow you can inspect yourself.

entry.title: The Maths Behind Polymarket binary-pairs arbitrage
entry.content:
Polymarket binary-pairs arbitrage looks for Polymarket YES and NO shares that together cost less than USD 1 after fees. That check fits on one line. Sizing the trade is harder: the displayed prices may cover only a few shares, fees can reduce the shares received, and the two orders can fill differently.

This post covers the general maths behind the Polymarket binary-pairs arbitrage project. The source code is not public. All prices and outcomes below are hypothetical examples for checking the arithmetic, not results from a live run.

Why a pair is worth USD 1

In a binary market, let the YES payout be $X$, so NO pays $1-X$. Holding one of each gives

$$ X+(1-X)=1. $$

The shares must belong to the same condition and form a complete set. YES on one question and NO on a similar question does not count. Polymarket's portfolio documentation describes merging a matching pair back into collateral.

Buying equal quantities $q$ at prices $p_Y$ and $p_N$, ignoring fees and other costs, gives the profit

$$ \pi(q)=q(1-p_Y-p_N). $$

Suppose YES costs USD 0.46 and NO costs USD 0.51. Buying 100 of each costs USD 97 and pays USD 100, a gross USD 3 spread. This assumes both sides fill at those prices and the set settles as expected.

Buy fees can leave fewer pairs than ordered

A first model subtracts a dollar fee from that USD 3. When fees come out of the shares received, the model must use the smaller net balances.

In a hypothetical model with fee rate $r$ and exponent $e$, the dollar fee per gross share at price $p$ is

$$ f(p)=r[p(1-p)]^e. $$

This is a parameterised example, not a universal fee schedule; check each market's actual fee rules.

Converting the fee into shares gives a retained fraction

$$ a(p)=1-\frac{f(p)}{p}. $$

If both orders buy $q$ gross shares at fixed prices, the net balances are $q,a(p_Y)$ and $q,a(p_N)$. The smaller balance limits the complete pairs:

$$ m=q\min{a(p_Y),a(p_N)}. $$

Valuing any unmatched remainder at zero gives a conservative paired profit before other costs:

$$ \pi_{\mathrm{pair}}=m-q(p_Y+p_N). $$

With the earlier prices and, for this example only, $r=0.02$ and $e=1$:

$$ a(0.46)=1-0.02(0.54)=0.9892, $$

$$ a(0.51)=1-0.02(0.49)=0.9902. $$

Ordering 100 shares a side leaves 98.92 YES and 99.02 NO, so only 98.92 complete pairs. Against the USD 97 cost, that leaves USD 1.92 before other costs. The 0.10 unmatched NO shares are valued at zero.

Over a range of possible fill prices, a conservative estimate uses the smallest retained fraction in that range. Fees and costs must use consistent units.

The cheapest price may cover only a small order

Suppose the asks are:

SidePriceShares available at that price
YESUSD 0.4620
YESUSD 0.5080
NOUSD 0.51100

The first 20 pairs cost USD 0.97 each before fees. Buying 100 YES means taking the next level too, so if the book holds, 100 shares a side cost

$$ C(100)=20(0.46)+80(0.50)+100(0.51)=100.20. $$

Even with no fees, the USD 100 payout leaves a USD 0.20 loss. Multiplying the best displayed prices by 100 would have shown a USD 3 profit.

A depth-aware calculation evaluates quantities at depth breakpoints, within budget and size limits. For size $q$, it finds the limit prices $L_Y(q)$ and $L_N(q)$ needed to reach it, giving a conservative cost bound

$$ C_{\max}(q)=q[L_Y(q)+L_N(q)]. $$

At $q=100$ this bound is USD 101; at $q=20$, USD 19.40. It charges every share at its leg's limit price, so it can exceed the cost from walking the book.

A profitable plan still needs two fills

The bounds above assume both legs fill in full. Execution does not guarantee that.

Suppose YES fills for 100 shares but NO for only 30. Ignoring fees to isolate the mismatch, the holdings are

$$ 100Y+30N=30(Y+N)+70Y. $$

Thirty complete pairs pay USD 30. The other 70 YES shares depend on the outcome or on the price when sold. Completing the hedge may mean paying more for NO than the plan allowed.

For net balances $n_Y$ and $n_N$, complete pairs are $\min(n_Y,n_N)$ and the unmatched quantity is $|n_Y-n_N|$. Submitted orders cannot establish either number; execution records must show what filled and what fees were deducted.

Stale data, mismatched token identities, or a missing leg can void a trade.

From a price observation to an execution record

The workflow should keep enough evidence to reconstruct each decision: both order books for the same condition, their observation times, and the fee parameters used. Reject a candidate if either book is too old.

Next, size the trade from executable depth and net shares after fees, and cap order cost and unmatched exposure before submitting. A positive spread alone says nothing about size or exposure.

After submission, track each leg separately: requested quantity, filled quantity, average fill price, fees deducted, and remaining quantity. Reconcile these with the resulting balances before counting pairs. An order acknowledgement confirms a request was received, not a fill.

These are general requirements for a paired-trade system, not a description of Polymarket binary-pairs arbitrage's private implementation.

What I would check in a paper-trading result

Polymarket binary-pairs arbitrage is in production and also supports paper trading: real market prices, simulated orders, and balances that persist across restarts. This section is about simulated results, not live returns.

A detected gap, a risk-approved decision, a simulated fill, and realised profit are different stages. To assess a run, I would check the observed prices and quantities, the book's age, the fee parameters, and how the simulator decided each order filled.

For a completed trade, the accounting covers paired collateral recovered, value from unmatched shares, purchase cost, and other execution costs:

$$ \pi_{\mathrm{net}}=M+U-C-K, $$

where $M$ is recovered paired collateral, $U$ is the unmatched inventory's proceeds or marked value, $C$ is purchase cost, and $K$ is other costs not already deducted. If $U$ includes unsold inventory, part of the figure is unrealised.

Before trusting a paper balance, I would compare its assumed fills with each leg's recorded depth and timestamps. A simulator that grants both fills at observed prices has assumed away the failure above.

entry.title: Trying to Understand PaperTrade's Tokenomics
entry.content:
PaperTrade caught my attention because losing traders receive PAPER, which they can stake for USDC rewards. You could lose on a trade and still come out ahead. I wanted to know how, where the USDC comes from, and why the next person would join.

Some people trade to profit from price moves; others may accept losses to accumulate PAPER. The mint rate also changes, so an early and a later participant can lose the same amount and receive different amounts of PAPER. Who benefits as more people join, and do the rewards keep attracting activity once they become less generous?

So I looked at how the LP pays winners, how losses become tokens, what stakers can claim, and the relayer, since a trader who can't close a position can't realize any of it.

I worked through this in a ChatGPT conversation, then checked the linked documentation and Guardian review. These notes cover the published design as of 21 October 2026, not every deployed contract or its live balances.

Who pays when you win?

PaperTrade creates synthetic trades against its own liquidity pool (LP), priced at the midpoint of Hyperliquid's best bid and ask. Your position doesn't become an order on Hyperliquid's perpetual order book; the LP takes the other side. The documentation describes BTC and ETH positions with multipliers up to 1,000×. Trading and pricing

Say you put $100 into a position at 100×, giving $10,000 of exposure. If the price moves 0.5% your way, the linear gross profit is $50. But PaperTrade applies an asymmetric impact adjustment to profitable closes, and that sum ignores liquidation and the other settlement rules, so it isn't what gets credited.

The LP needs USDC to pay that profit. PaperTrade's Martingaler mechanism lets the pool start without seed capital and build its bankroll from trading losses. If it cannot cover winning payouts, those payouts can wait. Martingaler overview

So a profitable trade can leave you waiting for money. The documentation splits the accounting into three parts:

StateWhat it records
TreasuryTracked LP funds under the settlement rules
sideBucketProceeds parked while the payout queue is active
Payout queueUnpaid winning profits, with older claims paid first

On a winning close, your margin returns to your available balance separately. Profit that cannot be funded goes into the queue, and later backing can pay those claims through a harvest process. Solvency and queue

In a simplified case, you're owed $5,000 of profit and only $1,000 can be paid now. The other $4,000 is still owed, but the queue doesn't create the USDC; you wait for backing.

Losing a trade earns PAPER

Eligible realized losses mint PAPER. The documented starting rate is 100 PAPER per dollar of eligible loss basis while tracked LP is below $2 million. Above that threshold, the rate decays using a high-water mark, so distributing funds out of the LP doesn't reset it to the earlier rate. Mint curve

The same eligible loss can earn different amounts of PAPER depending on timing. “Eligible” matters: the mint basis can differ from what a trader loses under the settlement rules.

Staked PAPER earns a share of eligible USDC distributions. The standard model has no lockup or cooldown, and rewards can be claimed into the Exchange balance before withdrawal. Staking and claims

A stake that stays at 1% of the pool while $50,000 is distributed receives $500. Compare that with what you spent acquiring PAPER. Your share can shrink as others stake, and one distribution doesn't predict the next.

This changes how I read volume. One person trades expecting BTC to rise; another accepts a loss to get PAPER. Both add volume for different reasons.

Guardian lists farming on gross losses, including hedged strategies, as a retained economic risk. A losing position can qualify for tokens while another position offsets some of that loss. Guardian security review

The liquidation rule needs a separate read

Liquidation through PaperTrade's hard-bust trigger takes the full isolated margin, even where a voluntary close at the trigger could still return some equity. The documentation describes a buffer of roughly five basis points of price. Liquidations

With a large position relative to margin, a small price difference can take much of your money. The ordinary closing calculation won't tell you what comes back after liquidation; the paths follow different rules.

Who submits the trades?

The user signs an instruction, and the relayer and batch executor submit it to the Exchange. Session-key and contract checks validate the authority behind it. Architecture

I can inspect what reaches the contract, not what happened to a request before that. Was it delayed? Rejected? Could I submit it another way?

Guardian's review flags relayer dependence and price bounds on signed instructions, and describes upgrade authority. The off-chain relayer, sweeper, and keepers were out of scope, so the review doesn't prove the submission service is fair or always available. Guardian security review

The protocol also documents a risk in using the instantaneous best-bid/ask midpoint: quote changes can move its reference price. Open-interest caps and adjustments to winning PnL limit exposure but don't remove the risk. Risk documentation

If the authorized relayer stopped submitting requests, how would I close my position? I'd want to see that fallback demonstrated.

Why would people join?

Early arrivals can earn PAPER at the earlier mint rate, stake it, and potentially receive USDC. If they share those rewards, others have a reason to look too. That's my reading; I don't know the team's marketing plan. I've left out the paid-promotion claims, launch figures, and wallet earnings from the original chat because I haven't verified them.

What I want to know is whether people keep trading once earning PAPER is less attractive. I would look at repeat participation after rewards decline, how concentrated the distributions are, and how much volume comes from identifiable farming. Counting wallets isn't enough, because one person can use several addresses.

entry.title: How I Define When a Payment Is Complete
entry.content:
I coordinate an engineering team building Web3 payments: I maintain the backlog and roadmap, run Scrum ceremonies, and clarify priorities with the business owner.

I start requirements with the users and how they will understand the flow. For a payment, I ask what the customer sees while waiting, and whether the status tells them to wait, retry, or act.

When the merchant can credit a payment

“Make deposits more reliable” leaves one decision open: which event lets the merchant credit its ledger?

I settle it with the business owner and engineers. In the documented CryptoRails flow, the browser detects incoming funds and shows the customer feedback. The merchant backend credits the ledger only after verifying the signed settlement webhook.

The trade-off: the payment is not complete until confirmation and server verification, so the interface has to show progress meanwhile. Treating detection as completion would let the screen promise what the backend has not verified.

What I put into acceptance criteria

That boundary changes what the team tests:

  • Deposit detection updates the interface without marking the payment settled.
  • A delayed confirmation leaves the payment pending.
  • The backend verifies the webhook before updating the ledger.
  • A repeated webhook or retry cannot credit the same payment twice.

A successful demo covers only one path, so I include the delayed and duplicate cases in the definition of done.

Keeping the scope deliverable

The request also needs agreed networks, failure cases, and user responses. I turn these into backlog items, track dependencies, and raise blocked work or competing requests with the business owner.

The CryptoRails workflow shows the deposit and consolidation sequence behind these requirements. Product-specific business, metric, and implementation details remain confidential.

Related reading

  • The CryptoRails deposit-to-settlement workflow.
  • Why a Web3 payment needs more than a transaction hash.

entry.title: TRON Energy Is a Product Requirement
entry.content:
On EVM networks, transactions normally need the native coin for gas. TRON token transfers use Energy and may consume Bandwidth. If an account lacks Energy, the transfer can burn TRX to cover the shortfall.

That changes the payment cost and what we must check before broadcast.

The payment sequence

We rent Energy before a resource-heavy TRON transaction:

  1. Validate the payment and network.
  2. Check the transaction’s resource requirement.
  3. Rent Energy when needed.
  4. Broadcast and monitor the transaction.
  5. Wait for the required confirmation condition.
  6. Reconcile the transfer with the payment request.

Requirements and testing

The backlog must cover insufficient resources, rental failure, unexpected costs, and confirmation delays. QA also needs chain-specific address, wallet, and fee cases.

I now check these requirements before the team designs error states. Exact rental rules and internal implementation details stay confidential.

entry.title: Why We Built an Internal CRM After Trying Salesforce
entry.content:
At Quandatics, I’m working on an internal CRM connecting sales, project delivery, and finance.

The choice to build internally

The team had tried Salesforce, but it needed workarounds around our process. We could keep adapting it, change our process, or build internally. We chose to build around the sales, delivery, and finance handoffs.

We control the handoffs, but we also own development, deployment, and support. An established CRM can be the better option when its process fits the business.

I map requirements around what each team needs before it can act: the approved scope, supporting documents, current status, and who owns the next step.

From lead to sales order

A qualified lead becomes an account, a contact, and an opportunity. An account can have several opportunities, each with its own sales funnel and approvals.

A won opportunity's approved quotation becomes a numbered sales order. The order links the sale to a project with its items, budget, team, phases, and milestones.

From delivery to payment

Each project phase has deliverables and a progress percentage. When a phase is done, the team submits a milestone claim with evidence, and management approves it before finance invoices.

The same records show delivery progress, billed amounts, receipts, and outstanding payments, so finance and delivery do not reconstruct the status separately.

From completed work to invoice-ready

Completed delivery and invoice readiness are different stages. A completed milestone describes the work; invoice readiness also depends on the supporting evidence and management approval finance needs to act.

I use this handover to connect the requirements of the three teams:

  • Sales: the approved scope provides the reference for what was agreed.
  • Delivery: the completed milestone and its supporting evidence explain what has been delivered.
  • Finance: the milestone claim and management approval provide the basis for issuing the invoice.

My contribution is translating those handovers into requirements and supporting implementation, testing, and feedback. The product work is not just recording that a task is complete. It is making the next team's required information, approval, and responsibility clear. Invoice-ready does not mean that an invoice has been issued or payment received.

Customer receipts and supplier costs

For customers, a milestone claim becomes a sales invoice, then a matched receipt. The accounting entry goes to Autocount with supporting documents.

For suppliers, a purchase order links to the sales order. Finance matches the supplier invoice to it, approves a payment voucher, and posts the cost to the project.

My role

I work across requirements, design, development, production deployment, and support. I clarify who owns each record, what each status means, and what happens when scope changes or approval is late.

For a milestone claim, I define the evidence and approval finance needs before invoicing. I settle ownership and approvals before adding fields or screens. Support shows the gaps, such as an incomplete claim or a late handover.

The internal CRM is in daily use, with further modules in development. Client-specific implementation details and operational results remain confidential.

entry.title: A Web3 Payment Needs More Than a Transaction Hash
entry.content:
A transaction hash identifies a submitted transaction. It does not tell the backend whether it can credit a ledger or release an order.

On a multi-chain gateway, I kept returning to one question: when can each person act on a payment state?

What each state needs to tell us

  • Customer: wait or retry?
  • Merchant: release the order or not?
  • Backend: is there verified evidence to update the ledger?
  • QA: what are the acceptance criteria for each transition?

Submission, confirmation, failure, and settlement need distinct meanings in the interface, webhook handler, and support process.

Detection and settlement

Client-side detection gives quick feedback when funds appear. Settlement needs a verified server-side signal that checks network, token, recipient, amount, transaction status, and duplicate processing.

Acceptance criteria I would write

  • Give each payment request a unique reference and expiry.
  • Check the selected token and network before signing.
  • Record the transaction hash without marking it settled.
  • Define separate responses for delays, failures, and duplicates.
  • Verify a webhook before it updates the ledger.
  • Prevent retries from crediting the same payment twice.

The CryptoRails lifecycle note covers the documented deposit and consolidation flow. These requirements are generalised; internal details and performance results remain confidential.

Related reading

  • Deposit detection, consolidation, and settlement in CryptoRails.
  • How I define when a payment is complete.

entry.title: A Small Talk About Hackathons
entry.content:
Hackathons demand an insane amount of time and energy. Preliminaries, semi-finals, and finals each mean more brainstorming, last-minute changes, and almost no sleep.

At first, I finished each one looking forward to the next. After enough rounds, I was tired before the next one started.

I also kept comparing myself to people who work in tech every day. I’m a mathematics student exploring outside my field, which is easy to forget when everyone seems more experienced.

One more hackathon is coming up. I’ll give it what I can, then take a proper break. I still want to do hackathons, but I need time away from constantly proving myself.

entry.title: Dead Internet Theory #1
entry.content:
LinkedIn and Reddit feel different lately. I keep seeing polished posts that say the right things but feel detached from any person. It may be a real shift, or my own overreaction.

I have used ChatGPT to help write before. Reading it back, it didn’t sound like anything I had lived. The sentences were clean; the experience was artificial.

Chatbots are good for proofreading, restructuring, and catching the sentence I somehow wrote twice. They should not supply the experience. I would rather read a long-ass, badly organised article by someone who was there than a perfect post assembled from general opinions.

I can’t tell if I’m seeing more bots, more generated content, or just noticing both more. If you’ve noticed it too, email me.

entry.title: Building a DeepSeek-R1 Chatbot
entry.content:
I built a chatbot with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B to try a downloadable reasoning model. The interface shows its intermediate output separately from the final response.

Try the Hugging Face demo or read the source.

Showing the intermediate output

The model produced reasoning text before its answer, so I displayed it instead of discarding it.

Asked about climate change in Malaysia, it gave a structured response that included the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and a “Ch bamboo” initiative I had never heard of. It sounded convincing despite those mistakes.

The intermediate text helped me inspect responses and compare prompts. It still needed fact-checking.

Hosting the experiment

I used Gradio on a basic Hugging Face Spaces instance with 2 vCPUs and 16 GB RAM, so the demo can be slow to respond.

The small model kept things manageable: I could download it, read the model card, and change the interface without a paid inference API.

Model details and published results are on the official model card; hosting is in the Spaces documentation.

entry.title: Eco Finance: A PayHack Prototype
entry.content:
Eco Finance shows estimated carbon emissions alongside everyday spending. We built it at PayHack 2024 as a 24-hour prototype using OpenFinance transaction data and dummy emission factors.

Estimating a transaction’s footprint

The proposed calculation multiplies the amount spent by an emission factor for the merchant category code (MCC). With a dummy factor of 0.5 kg CO₂ per RM, a RM 100 transaction comes to 50 kg CO₂.

Real use would need researched factors per merchant category. We considered surveys and work with DOSM; the hackathon version did not validate the estimates.

The proposed business model

We explored pooling estimated savings, certifying carbon credits, selling them to companies, and rewarding users, with Bursa Carbon Exchange as the market reference. This was a proposal to investigate, not an implemented or validated credit system.

What we built

We made a customer interface and an admin view. The demo is no longer maintained, so these screenshots are the record.

We didn’t make the final round T.T. I wrote more about the build, mentoring, and deadline problems in my first hackathon experience.

entry.title: First Physical Hackathon Experience
entry.content:
Janice, Roius, Gwyn, and I entered PayHack 2024 as four UTAR mathematics students. Two of us had done a hackathon, Gwyn had never coded, and none of us knew much web development.

We made the Top 32 of almost 100 teams, then had four days, around our internships, to learn enough Vue.js and Flask for a prototype. Janice travelled from JB to KL for it.

The idea and the questions we hadn’t answered

Our idea, MouManTai, estimated carbon footprints from transaction data and explored pooling the savings for trading.

Johan Nasir’s mentoring felt like a rotan session. “What happens if the carbon credits are manipulated?” “How do you ensure the footprint data is authentic?” Each one sent us back to our assumptions.

Keeping the demo alive

We did tutorials after our internships. At the hackathon we slept in turns; I couldn’t get a tent, so I took four-hour naps on a bench.

At 8:30 AM on submission day, 90 minutes before the deadline, our backend crashed while parsing data. We hardcoded some components and submitted by 10 AM.

The pitch

We didn’t make the Top 10. A blockchain remittance team stood out: they had researched regulation and validated their market as carefully as they built the product.

The stronger pitches tied features to business problems, survived demo pressure, and answered questions with numbers. Next time, I wanted to validate the market earlier and practise the pitch more.

I did win a Samsung monitor in the lucky draw, which gave our tired team a laugh.

Janice, Roius, and Gwyn took the risk with me. Johan asked the questions we wanted to avoid. PayNet and JomHack gave us a place to test an idea outside the classroom.
